passages.where: Jesus, in the Sermon on the Mount, speaks to ordinary people whose next meal and next coat were real questions. He does not tell them food and clothes do not matter. He points them to the birds and to a Father who feeds them, and asks what worrying has ever added.
The end of the same teaching. Jesus does not pretend tomorrow holds no trouble. He says today has enough of its own, and gives the reader permission to carry one day at a time.

Paul writes from prison to a church he loves, which is also under pressure and has two leaders at odds (Philippians 4:2). He does not simply tell them to stop feeling anxious. He tells them what to do with the anxiety: bring every request to God, with thanks, and he promises that God's peace will stand guard over their hearts and minds.

Peter writes to scattered Christians facing suffering and hostility. Casting anxiety on God comes in the same breath as humbling yourself under his hand: letting go of the strain of holding your life together alone, because he cares for you.
A psalmist surrounded by people doing wrong asks who will stand up for him, admits his foot was slipping, and says this: the anxiety was real and it was many, and God's comfort met him inside it.

God speaks to Israel, whom he calls “O worm of Jacob, O few men of Israel” a few verses later, while the nations around them tremble at a conqueror from the east. The reason not to fear is not that the danger is small but that God is with them and will hold them.

A psalm of David, by its heading from the time the Philistines seized him in Gath. He does not say he is never afraid. He says what he does when he is: “When I am afraid, I put my trust in You.” Fear and trust sit in the same sentence.

Experienced fishermen think they are about to drown while Jesus sleeps in the stern. Their question, “don't You care that we are perishing?”, is the question anxiety asks. Jesus answers the storm first, and then their fear.

Martha is serving guests in her own home and is upset that her sister sits listening to Jesus. Jesus names her state gently, “worried and upset about many things,” and points her to the one thing that cannot be taken from her.
The psalm ends with a prayer to be known all the way down, concerns included. It is the opposite of hiding the worry from God until it is under control.

misread.taken: This verse is sometimes used as if anxiety were a switch a faithful person can simply turn off, so that anyone who still feels anxious has failed, or is told that prayer should replace a doctor.
misread.says: Paul gives a practice, not a switch: prayer and petition, with thanks, about everything. What he promises is not that every request will be granted as asked, but that the peace of God will guard the heart and mind. Paul himself admits to sorrow, to being anxious, and to the daily pressure of his concern for all the churches (Philippians 2:27-28, 2 Corinthians 11:28). The verse calls a worried person toward God. It does not shame them for being worried, and nothing in it forbids getting medical help.

whole: Anxiety is often less a single fear than a weather system. It hums under the day and grows loud at night. It rehearses conversations that have not happened and disasters that may never come. Many people who carry it have already been told not to worry, and have found that being told does not help. Some have been told that it is a lack of faith, and now feel anxious and guilty at once.

The Bible is more honest than that. Its people are afraid often, and say so: David running for his life, the disciples in the storm, Paul under pressure from all the churches, Jesus in Gethsemane overwhelmed with sorrow. Scripture does not treat fear as strange. What it treats as the deeper trouble is the attempt to carry life alone, as if everything depended on staying ahead of every danger. Jesus' word about the birds is aimed there. The worry is not foolish because nothing can go wrong; it is too heavy because it was never meant to be carried without a Father.

So the Bible's answer is not a technique for feeling calm. It is a direction to turn. Bring the specific fear to God, in words, with thanks for what is still true. Do it again tomorrow, because tomorrow has its own trouble. Let the people around you carry some of it. Peace in the Bible is something that guards a person, not something they have to produce. When anxiety is heavy and long, a doctor or a counselor is one of the ways God's care reaches people, and seeking that help is not a failure of faith.

differ.share: Christians agree that anxiety is common to human life, that God invites anxious people to bring their fears to him, and that worry does not have the last word.

views.name: Mostly a spiritual matter
views.body: Some Christians teach that most anxiety is first a matter of trust, and that prayer, Scripture and the church are the main remedy, with medical help kept for severe cases.

views.name: Body and soul together
views.body: Others stress that a person is body and soul together, so that anxiety can have causes in the body as well as in belief, and that medicine and counseling belong alongside prayer from the start.

differ.after: Both say that God cares for the anxious and that no one should be left to carry it alone. The Honest Answer “Is my anxiety a spiritual failure?” takes this further.

sit: What is the one fear that keeps returning tonight, and what would it sound like to say it to God in plain words, with one thing you are still thankful for?

prayer.lead: Psalm 131 is short enough to pray in a few breaths. It ends by handing hope to God, now and later.
